lessons.title: Trace a Full TaskFlow Request
lessons.summary: Start at a user click, identify form/local state, the HTTP request, API validation, authentication, authorization, business rule, persistence call, database change, response, cache/UI update.
lessons.body:
Trace a Full TaskFlow Request

Why this matters
Start at a user click, identify form/local state, the HTTP request, API validation, authentication, authorization, business rule, persistence call, database change, response, cache/UI update. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Start at a user click, identify form/local state, the HTTP request, API validation, authentication, authorization, business rule, persistence call, database change, response, cache/UI update.
• For each boundary, state what is trusted and why.
• If you cannot identify the source of truth for a value, mark it as a learning target.
• This trace becomes the recurring map used across all 37 phases.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, framework readiness and taskflow preview stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter trace a full taskflow request again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.
objectives: Start at a user click, identify form/local state, the HTTP request, API validation, authentication, authorization, business rule, persistence call, database change, response, cache/UI update.
For each boundary, state what is trusted and why.
If you cannot identify the source of truth for a value, mark it as a learning target.
Use Trace a Full TaskFlow Request in a runnable example rather than only describing it.
Predict a result before execution and compare prediction with evidence.
Introduce one safe failure and diagnose the cause systematically.
setup: Create or reuse a disposable practice folder so experiments do not pollute the production TaskFlow tree.
Open the terminal and editor side-by-side. Keep browser DevTools visible for browser work.
Write the expected behavior in one sentence before adding code.
steps: Start two simulated searches with different delays. Reproduce a stale result, then guard the latest request or cancellation boundary.
Run the smallest version first. Capture exact terminal/browser/database output before adding a second concept.
Change one input, ordering, state transition, or configuration assumption. Predict the new output, then run it.
Explain the result in terms of runtime behavior, data flow, identity, or ownership—not “the framework did it”.
Rebuild the example once without looking at the completed version.

lessons.title: Choose Your Course Entry Point
lessons.summary: Complete this foundation if the prerequisite assessment reveals gaps; do not rush because framework complexity amplifies weak fundamentals.
lessons.body:
Choose Your Course Entry Point

Why this matters
Complete this foundation if the prerequisite assessment reveals gaps; do not rush because framework complexity amplifies weak fundamentals. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Complete this foundation if the prerequisite assessment reveals gaps; do not rush because framework complexity amplifies weak fundamentals.
• Experienced developers may skip modules they can demonstrate, not merely recognize.
• Phase 00 assumes you can read JavaScript/TypeScript, use Git/terminal, understand React basics, and reason about HTTP.
• Keep the foundation available as a reference when later errors reveal a missing mental model.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, framework readiness and taskflow preview stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter choose your course entry point again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.
